items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
PC Gamer reports:

The Australian STEM Videogame Challenge, a "free national videogame development competition for students," has confirmed that the rise of generative AI means this year's event will be the last...
Speculation as to the cause of the program's cancellation focused primarily on the presence of AI in entries: Another self-proclaimed judge said the problem wasn't merely the use of AI in itself but that "some students just completely generate their games with AI...." 

[T]he Australian Council for Educational Research has confirmed that the cancellation was in fact due to AI.... "making it harder to judge what students made themselves, and moving the program away from its original purpose."

items.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Misled Company Leaders On Affair With Chinese Businesswoman
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang misled several of the company's leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, about the nature of his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, with whom he had an affair, according to two people familiar with the matter and internal correspondence reviewed by Reuters. [...] During the autumn of 2025 and in October 2026, in response to press queries that drew some Nvidia leaders' attention to his relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, Huang at both times described their interactions as appropriate, the people said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Reuters only reviewed messages from the exchanges in October, not the ones from 2025. In two separate messages in October, Huang told Nvidia leaders, including Teter and Wagonfeld, that the interactions reflected standard business dealings with customers. In other messages, Huang affirmed the routine nature of his interactions with Megaspeed.
 
Nvidia's Huang also discussed taking legal action against the New York Times after it published an article in October of last year that drew attention to his meetings in public with Alice Huang, the people said. That article had prompted Jensen Huang to communicate with some Nvidia leaders in 2025 about their interactions, which he did not describe as an affair, the people said. Ultimately, neither Nvidia nor Huang filed a lawsuit against the paper. A spokesperson for the New York Times said the paper received no legal demand. It is unclear when his relationship with Alice Huang became intimate. Photos posted online and verified by Reuters show them together in the US, China and elsewhere, dating as far back as December 2023.

items.title: Shadow AI in the Workplace: Data Security Risks and Governance Strategies
items.author: Bittu Kumar
items.content:
A junior associate is sitting at their desk, trying to finish a 110-page agreement that has to be ready by 8:00 AM. The coffee has gone cold. After hours of reading the same pages, even simple clauses are becoming difficult to understand.

There is still a lot of work left, and very little time.

The associate opens a free AI chatbot on a personal phone and copies three clauses from the agreement. Within seconds, the tool provides a short summary. The work becomes a little easier, and the associate moves on to the next task.

But there is one problem. The law firm has already banned the use of public AI tools. Its computers block access to these websites, and employees have been warned not to use them for professional work. Yet the associate has found another way to access the same tool through a personal device.

The firm's system may show that its restrictions are working. But it cannot necessarily show what the associate has shared through a personal connection.

This is one way Shadow AI can enter a workplace. The employee may not intend to expose confidential information. They may simply be trying to finish an urgent task. But the information has still moved outside the organisation's control. And this raises a question that companies need to consider: If employees are still finding ways to use AI despite a workplace ban, is blocking access really enough to protect the organisation?

Understanding the Shadow AI Problem

Shadow AI refers to the use of artificial intelligence tools by employees without the knowledge or approval of their organisation. These tools may include public chatbots, AI writing assistants, browser extensions, coding tools and meeting transcription applications.

The problem is not limited to which tool an employee uses. It is also about what information they share with it.

An employee may upload a client document to get a summary, enter company data to prepare a report, or share a section of source code to find an error. These actions may appear harmless from the employee's point of view. However, the organisation may have no clear understanding of where that information goes, how it is stored or what happens to it after the task is completed.

Many companies have responded by restricting or blocking public AI platforms. Their concerns are understandable. Confidential information, customer records and business documents should not be shared with services that have not been properly assessed.

However, a restriction does not automatically change employee behaviour. If a company blocks an AI website but continues to expect employees to complete the same workload within the same deadlines, the reason for using AI does not disappear. Some employees may simply find another way to access it.

This is where the real problem begins. A company may successfully block an application on its office network while remaining unaware that employees are using the same application through personal phones, private accounts or other connections.

Banning AI may restrict access through official systems, but it does not necessarily stop its use. In some situations, it can move that use beyond the organisation's visibility.

The use of AI at work is growing faster than many organisations can introduce their own systems and policies.

These figures are important because they show that employees are not waiting for their organisations to introduce every tool they want to use. But they should be understood carefully: they show workplace AI adoption and the use of personal tools; they do not prove that corporate bans are the reason employees use them.

The reasons can be practical. A legal associate may want to understand a long agreement more quickly. A researcher may need to organise a large amount of information. A software engineer may want help finding an error in code. An employee preparing a presentation may use AI to create an initial draft.

In each case, the employee is trying to save time or complete a task more efficiently.

This does not make every use acceptable. Employees still have a responsibility to follow workplace policies and protect confidential information. But organisations also need to understand why employees are turning to tools that have not been approved.

A policy that only says "do not use AI" may not answer the questions employees face every day: Which tools can I use? What information can I share? What should I do when the approved system cannot handle my task?

When these questions remain unanswered, employees may make their own decisions. That is how a technology policy can become disconnected from actual workplace behaviour.

The incident became an important warning for companies considering the use of public AI platforms. It showed that sensitive information can leave an organisation through an ordinary workplace activity. An employee does not need to hack a system or deliberately attack a company. Copying information into an external chatbot can itself create a serious exposure.

Samsung's response included restrictions on generative AI use. The incident demonstrates why companies became concerned about employees using public AI tools. It does not, by itself, prove that bans push employees towards personal devices. That is a separate issue that organisations need to examine through evidence about employee behaviour.

There is another important point here. When information is entered into an external AI service, the organisation needs to understand the service's data practices.

Different AI providers have different terms and settings. Some services may use submitted content for model improvement under certain conditions, while others offer business arrangements with different data-retention and training terms. It would be incorrect to assume that every public AI service handles every prompt in the same way.

The concern is that employees using personal accounts may not know which terms apply to their information. The organisation may also have no contract, security review or clear process through which it can manage that risk.

What Is Actually at Risk?

For companies and legal institutions, Shadow AI is not just an IT concern. It can affect confidential information, legal responsibilities, customer trust and business interests.

1.⁠ ⁠Confidentiality and Attorney-Client Privilege

Legal professionals regularly work with sensitive information. This includes client communications, draft agreements, litigation strategies, personal records and documents that have not been made public.

Uploading such material to an external AI service without proper approval can create serious confidentiality concerns.

However, it is important to distinguish confidentiality from attorney-client privilege. Sharing privileged information with a third-party service does not automatically waive privilege in every situation. The legal result depends on the jurisdiction, the circumstances of disclosure, the service provider's access and the steps taken to maintain confidentiality.

Even where privilege is not automatically lost, sharing client information without proper safeguards may raise professional, contractual or ethical concerns.

For a law firm, the question should therefore not be limited to whether an AI tool gives a useful answer. It should also ask whether the information being shared is permitted to leave the firm's controlled environment.

2.⁠ ⁠Data Protection and Financial Penalties

The risk becomes more serious when employees share personal information through unapproved AI tools.

For example, a document may contain a client's name, address, financial details, identification information or other personal data. If that information is sent to an external service without appropriate safeguards, the organisation may face data-protection questions.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides for penalties for specified failures. Under its Schedule, failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breaches can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore. This does not mean that every employee's use of an AI chatbot automatically leads to that penalty. The relevant legal duties, facts and circumstances must be considered.

Similarly, under the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), certain serious infringements can attract fines of up to €20 million or 4% of the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

These figures show why organisations need to take the handling of personal information seriously. But financial penalties are only one part of the problem. A data incident can also affect customer confidence, business relationships and the organisation's reputation.

3.⁠ ⁠Loss of Trade Secret Protection

Companies often hold information that gives them an advantage over competitors. It may include source code, product designs, pricing strategies, financial models, customer information or future business plans.

Keeping such information confidential is an important part of protecting trade secrets.

If employees regularly enter this material into public AI tools without checking the provider's terms or the organisation's security arrangements, the company may weaken its ability to show that it took reasonable steps to protect the information.

The legal position will depend on the relevant law and circumstances. But the business concern is simple: information that was meant to remain inside the organisation may be shared with an external service without proper control.

Why Blanket Bans May Not Solve the Problem

Blocking AI websites may appear to be the easiest response. A company can restrict access through its network, issue a policy and warn employees against using unapproved tools.

But consider the earlier example of the junior associate. Blocking a website on a company laptop does not prevent the associate from opening the same website on a personal phone. A personal hotspot can also take the activity outside the company's network.

The organisation may see that its office systems are following the policy. It may not see what is happening elsewhere.

This creates a difference between controlling access and controlling actual use.

A company that provides approved AI tools can set rules about who can use them, what information can be shared and which security measures apply. It can also review usage through appropriate technical controls.

By contrast, when employees use personal accounts and devices, the organisation may lose access to important information about that activity. It may not know which tools are being used, what information has been shared or whether an incident has taken place.

This does not mean companies should allow every AI tool. Some uses should remain prohibited, especially where sensitive information cannot be adequately protected. But treating a ban as the complete solution overlooks the reasons employees may continue using AI.

The issue is not simply whether an organisation permits or prohibits AI. It is whether its policy gives employees a safe and practical way to complete their work.

A Practical Way Forward: From Bans to AI Governance

Companies need a system that protects information without ignoring the way employees actually work. This does not require unrestricted AI access. It requires clear rules, suitable tools and safeguards that match the sensitivity of the information.

1.⁠ ⁠Provide Approved Enterprise AI Tools

If employees are using public AI tools because they need help with everyday tasks, organisations should consider providing approved alternatives.

Enterprise AI services may offer different contractual and technical protections, including limits on data retention and commitments about whether customer inputs are used for model training. Some providers also offer Zero Data Retention (ZDR) arrangements.

However, companies should read the actual service terms instead of assuming that an enterprise label or ZDR promise guarantees complete privacy. They need to understand what data is retained, what logs are created, who can access the information and which settings are enabled.

The aim is to give employees a reliable tool for their daily work without making them depend on personal accounts or unapproved services.

2.⁠ ⁠Use Local AI Models for Highly Sensitive Information

Some work involves information that should not be sent to an external AI service. This may include sensitive source code, confidential legal strategy, certain client documents or important business information.

For such work, organisations can consider running AI models on their own infrastructure or within a controlled private environment.

Open-source model families such as Llama and Mistral may be considered for internal deployment, depending on the organisation's technical needs and resources. For particularly sensitive work, a disconnected or air-gapped system may offer an additional layer of protection.

But local deployment is not automatically safe. The organisation still needs to manage access, system security, updates and the information employees enter into the model.

3.⁠ ⁠Create a Clear Data Classification System

Employees should not have to guess whether a document can be shared with an AI tool. Organisations need to make these rules clear so that employees can understand what information is safe to share and what needs protection.

One practical way to do this is dividing information into three categories: public, internal and condidential.

Public information, such as published reports, press releases, and public case laws, can be used with apporved public or enterprise AI tools. Internal information, including routine meeting notes and general internal dragts, should only be used with AI tools approved under company policy. Confidential information, such as client records, personal data, contracts, source code and M&A information, requries greater care. Employees should use restricted tools or seek additional approval before sharing them.

This system should be easy to understand and connected to the organisation's existing confidentiality rules. Legal teams may need additional restrictions for privileged communications, litigation material and client documents.

4.⁠ ⁠Use Data Loss Prevention Tools

Data Loss Prevention (DLP) tools can help organisations identify and control the sharing of sensitive information.

For example, these tools can detect personal indentification numbers, financial details or confidential information in data being sent to external AI services. Depending on how the system works, it may block the request, flag it for review or remove senstive information before it reaches an external service.

These tools are not perfect. They may miss information or flag material that is harmless. They should therefore support, rather than replace, clear policies and employee awareness.

5.⁠ ⁠Make Employees Part of the Process

Even a well-designed policy can fail if employees do not understand how to follow it in their daily work.

Organisations should explain which AI tools are approved, what information must not be shared, when human review is required and how employees can request access to a new tool.

They should also create a simple way for employees to report accidental disclosure. If people are afraid to report mistakes, organisations may learn about incidents too late to respond effectively.

At the same time, employees must remain responsible for following the rules. Practical alternatives do not remove the duty to protect confidential information. Organisations need both clear expectations and fair accountability.

Shadow AI is not going to disappear simply because an organisation blocks access to certain AI tools. Employees still have deadlines, daily tasks and work to complete. When approved tools are unavailable or difficult to use, some may look for other ways to get the same work done.

This creates a problem for organisations. They may have rules against using unapproved AI services, but those rules do not necessarily tell them where employees are actually using AI or what information they are sharing.

This does not mean employees should be free to use any tool they want. Confidential information still needs protection, and employees must take responsibility for how they use AI. But organisations also need to look at why employees are turning to tools outside the approved system.

If a tool is helping employees complete routine work more easily, the organisation should consider whether it can provide a safe alternative. It should also make clear what information can be shared and where approval is required.

The real issue is not just whether employees are following AI policies. It is whether those policies work in the way people actually do their jobs. If organisations want to manage Shadow AI, they need to understand its use rather than simply try to stop it.

items.title: Amazon's Plan to Index the World's Online Shopping Data
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Amazon is considering a "World Product Graph" that would index information about products sold across the internet in an effort to keep shoppers and AI agents from turning to Google, Reddit or other sources for product research. The proposed database could also improve Amazon's AI shopping assistant by addressing inaccurate or incomplete answers and allowing it to use cheaper models.
 
"Amazon cannot be the go-destination for every shopping mission if customers must leave to research product relationships on Google, brand websites, and review sites," according to an internal Amazon document. "These answers exist, but the only way to find them has been to leave Amazon for painstaking research on brand websites, third party review sites and tech forums." Reuters could not determine if or when this plan may be implemented, though the document, written like a press release, has an aspirational future release date of October 1, 2027.
 
Amazon said in a statement: "Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn't necessarily reflect our current plans. We're constantly working on new ideas and technologies to make Amazon's product catalog comprehensive, accurate, and helpful for customers."

items.title: How I Built an AI Marketing Team With Grok Bot Without Writing Code
items.author: Sam Brovda
items.content:
A non-engineer’s notes on running marketing with Grok Bot: one job per bot, a rules file every job reads, and nothing goes out without me

Last time I wrote about building a consumer mobile app on nights and weekends with AI coding agents.

The code was only half the problem. An app nobody hears about is a hobby. And I don’t have a marketing team.

So I built one out of bots. I use Grok Bot, where each bot has its own computer and can run jobs on a schedule. Here’s how it’s set up and what I’ve learned so far.

My first instinct was one big assistant that does everything. That’s like hiring one rep to prospect, run demos, do legal, and forecast. Nothing gets done well.

So every bot gets one job, written at the top of its instructions.

  • owns content ideas. Every weekday morning it pitches a few ranked ideas for short-form video and carousel posts, recommends one to make today, and drafts it when I say go.
  • checks the other bots every weekday before 8am. It reads what they actually produced, not what they say they did, and marks each one on track, slipping, or stalled.
  • When I need a new one, I describe the job and it writes the instructions: one job, one voice, and a list of things the bot must never do.

That last list matters more than the job itself. It’s the same lesson from coding agents. An agent with no boundaries will happily do things you never asked for.

The marketing bot never posts, comments, or messages anyone. It drafts. I post.

That one rule removes most of the risk. A bad draft costs me thirty seconds. A bad post under my name costs a lot more.

It’s approval tiers again. A rep can draft the proposal. They can’t sign the contract.

A rules file every job reads first

The marketing bot has one rules file, and every job reads it before doing anything. It holds the guardrails and a lessons section.

The guardrails are short:

  • No spending. No ads, no paid tools, no paid creators.
  • Never invent quotes, stats, or customers. Every quote gets a link and a date.
  • Check factual claims against a real source.
  • Only make product claims that are true today.

Then once a week, the Friday report adds a few plain lessons to the bottom. These are real ones from the first week:

  • We couldn’t count signups, because there’s no signup page yet. So signups stay “unknown,” never a guess.
  • Check every post about an hour after it goes up. One post sat at zero views and nobody noticed.
  • Log every post the same day it goes up. Two posts were only found later.

Then I changed the goal. Since there’s no signup page, posts stopped asking people to sign up. Now they close on a follow or a comment prompt. The bot wrote that change into the same file, with the date, so every job picks it up the next morning.

If you read my last piece, this will sound familiar. It’s the same idea as the instruction file for my coding agent. If a decision only lives in a chat, the next run won’t know about it.

Early on, the marketing bot built a content bank: 21 days of posts, planned out, so I’m never starting from a blank page.

That’s the real win for me. Not that the bot is creative. That I don’t have to decide what to post every single day. I review a plan, say yes or no, and move on.

Bots drift. They’ll report “done” on things that half-happened.

So the chief of staff bot doesn’t trust the reports. It reads the actual output. If a bot is off track, it nudges that bot once with the goal, what’s missing, and the next step. If it’s still off the next day, it flags it to me.

Its rules say never invent progress or metrics, and mark anything it can’t verify as unverified. I want a pipeline review, not a happy-ears forecast.

What I’d tell another non-engineer

You don’t need a marketing team to start. You need a few narrow bots and a way to catch them when they’re wrong.

For me that’s four things. One job per bot. A list of things each bot must never do. A rules file that collects lessons with dates. And nothing goes out under my name without my yes.

Even this post works that way. A bot drafted it from the work we actually did, and it doesn’t go up until I approve it.

I’m Sam Brovda. I come from enterprise sales and write about building software as a non-engineer.

items.title: How to Watch the Hunger Games Movies in Chronological Order
items.author: Jose
items.content:
So, full disclosure, I don’t really believe in watching movies in chronological order the first time around. I think that watching them by release date is usually the best way to go. However, if you’re planning on doing it for the Hunger Games movies, I’ve got you covered. Here are all the Hunger Games movies in chronological order.

Hunger Games Movies in Chronological Order

  1. The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes
  2. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping
  3. The Hunger Games: Catching Fire
  4. The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1
  5. The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 2

1. The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes

The first movie in the Hunger Games’ timeline, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes sees a young Coriolanus Snow trying to navigate the craziness that is the country of Panem. He eventually finds himself actively involved in the 10th annual Hunger Games as a mentor for District 12’s female tribute, Lucy Gray Baird.

Snow wants to be on top of the world, which means he’ll do anything and everything to see his dream realized. Cheat, kill, backstab - nothing is off limits if it means inching closer and closer to the top.

2. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Set 40 years after the events of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, it focuses on District 12 male tribute Haymitch Abernathy as he is forced to compete in the 50th Hunger Games. This time, though, the rules have changed. Every 25th Hunger Games, a new concept is added to make that year’s game even more special.

So, for the 50th Hunger Games, they decide to double the number of tributes. 48 in total, 4 from each district. It’s hard enough to win a normal Hunger Games, but to do it with double the people is damn near impossible. Haymitch will have to overcome the overwhelming odds if he wants to survive.

Fast forward 24 years, and we arrive at the 74th Hunger Games. Yes, the Hunger Games are still going, but the 12 Districts that are forced to send their children to death every year are sick and tired of it all. Revolution is coming. All it needs is for someone to light the fire.

In the midst of all this, District 12 teenager Katniss Everdeen volunteers to participate in the Hunger Games in place of her little sister. Alongside District 12 male tribute Peeta Mellark, Katniss will have to train and learn the inner workings of the games to outlast the other tributes and make it back home to her family.

4. The Hunger Games: Catching Fire

The fire of rebellion is spreading, and the government of Panem knows that it has to do something before it spreads too far. Katniss, who survived last year’s games, is seen as a dangerous individual who’s fanning the flames. President Snow decides that something has to be done about her and the other former Hunger Games victors.

For the 75th Hunger Games, a new special concept is added. Katniss and 23 other former Hunger Games winners will return to compete to the death. Knowing that they’re beloved by the populace, they tug at their heartstrings to try and get out of the games, further pushing people to revolt.

5. The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1

The rebellion is in full swing following the games, and Katniss, whether she wants to or not, is seen as the face of it. Most of the districts are quick to join her side, but President Snow won’t go quietly into that good night. He still has a few tricks up his sleeve, including brainwashing someone who’s very close to Katniss. I can’t go into more detail without spoiling the movie, but this is where things get serious. And they only get more serious in the following and final movie.

6. The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 2

The war between the rebellion and President Snow is finally coming to an end. All the districts are united against him; the only thing left to do is to storm the Capitol and to take down the president himself. But President Snow refuses to lose gracefully. Throughout the city, he has laid out traps for Katniss and her team. They’ll have to do their best to avoid these dangerous pods and make it to Snow’s mansion in one piece.

The Hunger Games are often lumped with other YA novel adaptations from that era, but I think that this film series is far and away one of the best in its genre. If you’re watching these movies for the first time, I encourage you to do it by release date. However, if you think it best to go by timeline order, I hope this Hunger Games in chronological order list serves you well.

items.title: How to Evaluate Snowflake Cortex Embedding Models for Enterprise Search
items.author: Akshay Sharma
items.content:
A company has 500,000 support tickets sitting in Snowflake. Years of troubleshooting notes, product defects, workarounds, resolutions, and occasional messages that just say "fixed after restart." Very helpful, thanks.

Someone wants an AI assistant that can search those tickets and suggest resolutions. The architecture looks straightforward. Take the documents, generate embeddings, store vectors, retrieve similar records, and let an LLM write the answer.

A few SQL queries later, you have a demo.

Then someone asks which embedding model you picked.

And there it is. We've designed an intelligent search system using the same decision-making process people use to buy televisions. Snowflake Cortex offers eight built-in text embedding models through . Some produce 768-dimensional vectors, others 1,024. Some are English-focused. Others support multiple languages. Context windows vary considerably.

The problem isn't a shortage of options.

It's figuring out what actually matters.

I've spent about eight years working with Snowflake, and one lesson from enterprise data engineering keeps showing up: the technically impressive option isn't necessarily the right one for your workload. Embedding models are no exception.

According to Snowflake's documentation, the built-in text embedding lineup includes:

snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5

snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0

snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0-8k

Snowflake also supports image embeddings through , but that's a different use case. We're keeping this investigation focused on text.

Eight models sound like eight chances to get it right. Or eight chances to explain to your architect why you chose one based on a name.

Let's narrow down the questions.

Round 1: 1,024 dimensions versus 768

The first temptation is obvious.

A 1,024-dimensional embedding contains more numbers than a 768-dimensional embedding. More numbers must mean more meaning. Unfortunately, vector search doesn't work like upgrading a laptop from 16 GB to 32 GB of RAM.

An embedding model learns a representation of language. Its dimensions are coordinates in that learned space, not a score for intelligence.

A larger representation might capture useful distinctions. It might also deliver no measurable improvement on your particular documents.

Imagine three fictional incident records:

  • Payment reconciliation failed after an upstream schema change.
  • Settlement processing rejected records following a column modification.
  • The finance department completed its quarterly budget review.

"Why did settlement reconciliation fail after the column changed?"

A useful model should recognize that A and B are relevant, while C is mostly unrelated.

But here's the interesting part. Suppose a 768-dimensional model puts B first, while a 1,024-dimensional model puts A first.

You can't answer that from the dimension count. Maybe both are valid. Maybe one describes the exact failure while the other concerns an older version of the pipeline. Maybe neither contains the accepted resolution.

The model's job isn't to produce a beautiful vector.

It's to retrieve useful evidence.

For an English-only knowledge base containing relatively short documents, I'd start with a compact model such as Arctic Embed M v1.5 as a baseline.

Then I'd test whether a larger model improves retrieval.

Round 2: The multilingual trap

Now the support organization expands.

Some tickets are in English. Others are in Spanish, French, Japanese, or a combination of languages.

"El proceso de conciliación falló después de modificar una columna."

"Why did reconciliation fail after the column update?"

Ideally, your retrieval system can connect these without requiring every ticket to be translated first. This is where models such as , Arctic Embed L v2.0, and Voyage Multilingual 2 become candidates.

But multilingual support comes with an uncomfortable question. Does supporting multiple languages mean equally good retrieval in every language?

A model can support multilingual embeddings and still perform differently across languages, technical domains, and query styles.

  • An English question against Spanish documentation.
  • A Spanish question against English documentation.
  • Mixed-language incident descriptions.
  • Product names that should never be translated.
  • Technical identifiers embedded inside ordinary sentences.

An error such as should remain , regardless of the surrounding language.

A model that understands a Spanish sentence but loses the exact error identifier hasn't solved the whole problem. I'd also separate two questions: can the model retrieve semantically similar information across languages, and does the retrieved information actually answer the user's question?

They're related, but they're not identical. Multilingual support earns a model a place in the evaluation. It doesn't automatically win the contract.

Round 3: The 32,000-token temptation

Next comes document length.

Consider a 40-page incident report. It contains the original failure, several failed fixes, the successful workaround, and a postmortem written two weeks later.

A model with a short context window can't embed the whole document in one pass. A model supporting longer inputs gives you more room.

Arctic Embed L v2.0 8K supports longer inputs than its standard version. Voyage Multilingual 2 supports up to 32,000 tokens. At first glance, longer sounds better. Fewer chunks. Less processing logic. Everybody goes home early.

Except there's a problem.

That 40-page report isn't necessarily about one thing.

The first section describes ingestion. The second discusses schema evolution. The third explains a permissions issue. The fourth says the original root-cause theory was wrong. Put everything into one vector and you're asking the model to summarize several distinct concepts into a single location in embedding space.

Now imagine a user searching specifically for the permissions issue.

Will the document-level vector represent that section strongly enough? Maybe. But I wouldn't bet the retrieval architecture on it.

Chunking exists for a reason. Sometimes a focused 300-token chunk retrieves better than an entire document represented by one embedding. Sometimes larger context helps preserve the explanation that a smaller chunk would lose.

The answer depends on the structure of the content.

I'd compare different chunking strategies before spending time arguing about context-window sizes. The bigger window may be useful. It isn't permission to stop thinking about document structure.

Round 4: Let SQL do some work

One thing I like about the Cortex approach is that generating a text embedding doesn't require standing up a separate model-serving application.

Snowflake provides .

SELECT AI_EMBED(
    'snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5',
    'An upstream schema change caused payment reconciliation to fail.'
) AS EMBEDDING;

The function returns a vector.

Let's use a small fictional knowledge base.

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE INCIDENTS (
    INCIDENT_ID NUMBER,
    DESCRIPTION VARCHAR
);

INSERT INTO INCIDENTS VALUES
(1, 'Payment processing failed after a schema modification.'),
(2, 'An upstream column change broke settlement reconciliation.'),
(3, 'The finance team completed its quarterly budget.'),
(4, 'A scheduled batch job exceeded its memory allocation.');

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE INCIDENT_VECTORS AS
SELECT
    INCIDENT_ID,
    DESCRIPTION,
    AI_EMBED(
        'snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5',
        DESCRIPTION
    ) AS EMBEDDING
FROM INCIDENTS;

WITH QUERY_VECTOR AS (
    SELECT AI_EMBED(
        'snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5',
        'Why did settlement reconciliation fail after a column change?'
    ) AS EMBEDDING
)
SELECT
    I.INCIDENT_ID,
    I.DESCRIPTION,
    VECTOR_COSINE_SIMILARITY(
        I.EMBEDDING,
        Q.EMBEDDING
    ) AS SIMILARITY
FROM INCIDENT_VECTORS I
CROSS JOIN QUERY_VECTOR Q
ORDER BY SIMILARITY DESC
LIMIT 3;

That's the basic mechanism.

For this illustrative example, we're calculating similarity against a tiny table. It's not a proposed production retrieval architecture for millions of documents.

More importantly, this SQL demonstrates to retrieve candidates, not whether the chosen model retrieves the candidates.

Those are two different problems.

And no, I haven't run this example across all eight models and discovered a secret winner. There are no fabricated benchmarks hiding behind the curtain.

The goal here is to make the model-selection process understandable and reproducible.

Round 5: When the nearest neighbor is still wrong

Here's my favorite trap in semantic search.

"How do I resolve error ERR_RECON_042?"

The system retrieves a document discussing reconciliation errors.

Great semantic match. Wrong error code.

The correct document contains , but a different document talks about similar failures in more natural language. The embedding model prefers the descriptive document. Now the LLM receives the wrong evidence and writes a perfectly polished answer.

We've successfully automated being confidently incorrect.

This is why I wouldn't build enterprise retrieval around vector similarity alone. Exact identifiers, error codes, schema names, version numbers, and product IDs often deserve lexical matching. Semantic search helps when people describe the same problem differently. Keyword search helps when the exact characters matter. Both can be useful.

Cortex Search supports hybrid retrieval, making it worth evaluating for applications that need semantic and lexical matching together.

The right question isn't always "Which embedding model should I use?"

Sometimes it's "Why am I asking an embedding model to solve a problem that exact matching handles better?" A screwdriver isn't a bad tool because it struggles with nails.

Round 6: The migration nobody budgeted for

Let's say you've embedded two million documents using snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5.

Six months later, a new model looks promising. Someone changes the model name used to generate query embeddings.

The stored documents were embedded with the old model. Your queries now use a different model. Even if two models return vectors with identical dimensions, their embedding spaces aren't necessarily compatible. And if one returns 768 dimensions while the other returns 1,024, the mismatch is even more obvious.

So switching models isn't just a configuration change.

You may need to regenerate embeddings for the corpus, maintain parallel indexes, measure retrieval changes, and coordinate the cutover.

  • The embedding model identifier.
  • The embedding version or generation configuration.
  • The source document version.
  • The time the embedding was generated.

This may sound like too much metadata for a vector. Until someone asks why search behavior changed last Tuesday. Then suddenly everyone loves metadata.

If I were evaluating embedding models for a real enterprise application, I wouldn't start with a leaderboard.

I'd start with a set of questions and known relevant documents. For an initial experiment, something like 100–200 representative queries could help expose failure patterns, although broader testing would be needed before making general performance claims.

I'd include straightforward questions, ambiguous queries, similar-but-wrong incidents, multilingual examples, and cases with no valid answer. Then I'd compare candidate models against the same data.

Here's the scorecard I'd use:

Did the correct evidence make the top five?

How high did the first relevant result appear?

Were the most relevant results ranked appropriately?

How quickly can the model process a search query?

What does it cost to embed the document collection?

How expensive is a future model migration?

What kinds of questions does the model get wrong?

I'd measure actual costs using Snowflake's current pricing and usage information rather than infer them from vector dimensions. And I'd pay special attention to the failures.

Suppose Model A retrieves the correct document for 94 out of 100 questions. Model B succeeds on 96.

What were those two extra questions?

A routine FAQ? Or an incident where retrieving an outdated fix could cause another production outage?

Raw accuracy alone doesn't tell you which failure matters more.

That's the problem with declaring winners before understanding the workload.

One more thing: your trial account might disagree

There's a practical issue worth mentioning. You can have unused Snowflake trial credits and still be blocked from calling certain Cortex embedding functions.

For example, a trial account may return an error indicating that an internal embedding function isn't available. That isn't proof that the SQL syntax is wrong or the requested model doesn't exist.

Account eligibility, regional availability, permissions, and service access all matter. Before writing a benchmark, verify that the account can actually invoke the candidate models. It's a small step that can save an afternoon of debugging the wrong thing.

After looking at the options, here's how I'd approach model selection.

  • For short, mostly English documents: Start with a compact English-focused baseline such as Arctic Embed M v1.5. Move to larger models when measured retrieval quality justifies it.
  • For multilingual content: Evaluate , Arctic Embed L v2.0, and Voyage Multilingual 2 against actual cross-language queries.
  • Test longer-context models, but compare them against sensible chunking strategies.
  • For error codes and technical identifiers: Don't force embeddings to do everything. Evaluate hybrid retrieval.
  • For enterprise deployment: Track model versions and plan for re-embedding before somebody decides to swap models on a Friday afternoon.

And for every category, verify model availability, pricing, and restrictions in your Snowflake region.

This isn't a universal ranking. It's a shortlist of where I'd begin testing.

Snowflake Cortex makes generating embeddings easy. Choosing the right model is still your responsibility.

Eight models don't mean eight levels of intelligence. A larger vector doesn't guarantee a better match. A longer context window doesn't eliminate chunking. And multilingual support doesn't guarantee that every language or technical domain performs equally well.

A model can retrieve something semantically similar and still miss the evidence your application needs. That's the part worth testing.

If I had to make the decision tomorrow, I'd start with a simple baseline, build a representative evaluation set, and bring in more capable models only when they solve a measured problem.

Because the embedding model isn't supposed to win a beauty contest.

It's supposed to find the right document. And when it doesn't, I'd much rather know that before the LLM writes three paragraphs explaining the wrong answer.

Author’s note: The scenarios and SQL examples in this article are illustrative. They are not drawn from confidential systems, and no comparative benchmark results are claimed.

items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a "general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode." By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
 
[...] Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there's a catch, he said. "The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems," he explained. "That is, you can't just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work." For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode
value must be 0 or 1." Of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement. Microsoft said in a statement that it was investigating the vulnerability and had no evidence it was being exploited in the wild. The company also said Defender blocks potential exploitation attempts.

items.title: How AI Agents Shape Human Judgment Through Analytical Assumptions
items.author: Dmitry Zaytsev
items.content:
A founder asks an AI agent to recommend which customer accounts deserve more attention. The agent checks revenue, support costs and renewal dates, then returns a sensible ranking. The numbers are accurate. The founder reviews the list and approves it.

But somewhere along the way, the agent decided what “deserve more attention” meant. Perhaps it prioritised immediate revenue over customers with growth potential. Perhaps it treated support requests as costs rather than evidence that a customer needed help.

The founder checked the answer. The objective behind it received less attention.

This is a harder problem than catching a hallucination. Nothing needs to be false for a recommendation to carry a choice that the person receiving it never consciously made.

When the calculation works

Anthropic published research on 27 October examining how agents influence experts’ judgement calls. Fifty professional analysts used Claude Code to assess a farming advisory programme. Researchers secretly assigned each agent a preference between defensible analytical options, including how to measure productivity.

Across four analytical choices, participants followed their agent’s assigned preference 86% of the time. The agents were instructed to make an honest case, not to deceive.

The limits matter. This was one task, in one field, with deliberately strengthened agent preferences. It does not establish how often the same thing happens inside companies. It does show why checking whether an analysis is technically sound may leave an important question unanswered: who selected the assumptions that made this answer persuasive?

An agent can help us reason while also steering what we consider reasonable.

The decision inside the metric

Consider a company asking AI to identify employees at risk of leaving. Before anyone discusses the accuracy of the predictions, several choices have already entered the task.

Is every departure something the company wants to prevent? Should attention go to people whose replacement would be expensive, people with scarce capabilities, or people whose development has stalled? What happens when the best next step for an employee is outside the organisation?

Different answers could produce different recommendations from the same information. None can be settled simply by making the model more accurate.

For me, this is where conversations about human capability become practical. We ask people to exercise judgement, but then present them with a finished recommendation in which the most consequential choices have already been made.

A manager might carefully inspect the evidence for contacting one employee without ever questioning why another employee was excluded from consideration. Their review can be diligent and still begin too late.

Make the alternatives visible

Before running a consequential analysis, the person responsible should write down what they want to achieve and what they are unwilling to sacrifice. It can be a short paragraph. The value comes from making the choice explicit enough to question.

For the customer example, that might mean preserving long-term relationships while reducing avoidable support work. That instruction would lead to different questions from simply asking which accounts are most profitable.

The agent can then help identify reasonable alternatives. What changes if we prioritise growth potential? Which customers move down the list if service costs carry more weight? What evidence would justify choosing one approach over another?

Suppose both approaches produce accurate forecasts. One favours an established customer with predictable revenue; the other favours a smaller account that requires investment. The useful conversation is about the company's commercial priorities and obligations. Asking the agent to check its arithmetic again will not resolve that choice.

This makes the disagreement available for discussion. A polished recommendation alone can conceal it.

The same principle belongs in the review. Ask which assumptions materially affected the result, rather than requesting a reassuring explanation of why the result is correct. A useful explanation should make it possible to disagree.

Keep a record of the choice

Teams already document outputs, approvals and actions. For important decisions, I would also keep a brief record of the objective selected, the alternative rejected and the reason for rejecting it.

This need not become paperwork attached to every routine task. It matters where a choice affects someone’s opportunities, commits significant resources or establishes a rule that will be applied repeatedly.

Later, if the outcome disappoints, the team can examine whether the calculation failed or whether it pursued the wrong objective. Those require different corrections. Without that distinction, companies can spend months improving a system’s performance against a goal nobody clearly endorsed.

There is room here for AI to improve our judgement. It can help us explore alternatives and notice consequences we would otherwise miss. But that benefit depends on leaving the choices open long enough for people to examine them.

Before approving the next recommendation, ask the agent to show you one reasonable alternative that would change the outcome. Then decide which approach you can defend to the people affected.
