items.title: Building a Multi-Agent Website Launch Validator With OpenMinion
items.author: Alan De Bortolo
items.content:
I run a small web agency. We build and host websites for small businesses in the US and Brazil, and every launch has the same floor: a title and a description, a canonical URL, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, icons, a sitemap, a 404 page that really returns 404, an , and a that does not lock AI search crawlers out. For years we checked that list by hand, one tab per item.

For Cortensor Hackathon 5, I turned the checklist into an agent called , built on OpenMinion 0.1, the agent SDK from the Cortensor ecosystem. It answers one question: is this site ready, ready with warnings, or blocked? The code is MIT-licensed at github.com/DesignMaster-Solutions/golive-gate and there is a 2-minute demo at youtu.be/tVH-x62QV3I.

This post is about the one design decision that made it trustworthy, and about what it looks like to run an agent on open, swappable inference instead of one vendor's API.

The rule: the model never fetches anything

The tempting version of this agent is one prompt: "here is a URL, tell me if it is ready". That version hallucinates. It will tell you a sitemap exists because sites usually have one.

So Go-Live Gate is split in three agents with different powers:

  1. It can call three read-only tools: , and . They are plain with 15-second timeouts and they return facts only (title length, which Open Graph tags exist, which bots blocks, the HTTP status of a random missing path). If the model skips a tool, the gap is filled deterministically, so the next step never guesses.
  2. It gets the raw facts and must return a pydantic-validated : a verdict plus one row per check with the evidence and the fix. The judge has no tools at all. It cannot fetch, so it cannot invent.
  3. A third agent must call , a tool marked . OpenMinion routes that call through a human approval callback (an interactive y/N, or for CI). If the human says no, nothing is written.

Every run writes next to . A reviewer can open both and check the model's verdict against what the tools actually saw. That file is the whole point: the agent is only as honest as the layer under it, and that layer has its own offline tests against a local HTTP server.

class Check(BaseModel):
    name: str
    status: Literal["pass", "warn", "fail"]
    evidence: str   # the fact from a tool result that justifies the status
    fix: str = ""

class GoLiveReport(BaseModel):
    site: str
    verdict: Literal["ready", "ready_with_warnings", "blocked"]
    checks: list[Check]
    summary: str

Why this matters for decentralized inference

When the facts live in code and the model only reasons over them, the model becomes replaceable. That is what makes open inference practical for a business tool.

OpenMinion talks to any OpenAI-compatible provider. Our recorded runs used a free open-weight model (nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free through OpenRouter); the same project is set up for the Cortensor Portal with one command (setup --provider cortensor-portal). I did not have to rewrite prompts or tools to switch. The judge's output is validated by a schema either way, so a weaker or slower node fails loudly instead of quietly writing a wrong verdict.

If you are building on a decentralized inference network, you cannot assume the same model, the same latency or the same token limits on every call. Designing the agent so that the model is the least trusted part is how you get repeatable results anyway.

The hackathon asked for building blocks tested and lessons learned, and these were the useful ones:

  • Read-only tools still asked for confirmation. A tool tagged and still came back as "Policy confirmation required ... reply yes", because the decorator default wins over the tags. Declaring fixed it.
  • The first request of every turn was not my agent. It was the automatic memory extractor, carrying the whole system prompt but exposing only one tool, . A model replaying that request alone said "the inspection tools are not available", and I spent an hour thinking my tools were hidden. A top-level "brain": {"auto_fact_extraction": {"enabled": false}} in removes that round trip.
  • One turn did not fit a free tier. With default tools, the main turn sent about 17k characters of system prompt plus eight built-in tools. Groq answered at 8,683 tokens. Free tiers also need pacing the SDK does not have (its retry waits 300 ms; the rate window is 60 s), so I wrapped the adapter to stay under 6.5k tokens per minute.
  • is not enforced on the model. The judge once answered with a markdown table. A JSON schema at the end of the instructions changed nothing; the same schema inside the user message worked on the first try.
  • in the same session lost the first message, so retries now resend the facts.

And one bug was mine. The first live run flagged a 697-character title on a client site whose real title is 63 characters. My parser was concatenating the elements inside inline SVG icons. The agent repeated what the tool reported, which is exactly why the facts layer has regression tests and the model does not get the last word.

On capegraniteconnection.com, a site we built, the gate returned with 11 checks: title 63 characters, description 149, canonical present, all four Open Graph tags, 12 JSON-LD types including LocalBusiness and FAQPage, , both icons, no AI crawler blocked, a sitemap with 44 URLs, a 3,902-byte , and a real 404. On a free model the investigator took 232 seconds and the judge 355. Slow, but it runs unattended before every launch, and it is cheaper than the hour of tabs it replaces.

python3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python -m unittest test_checks -v
.venv/bin/python gate.py yoursite.com --auto-approve yes

The lesson I would carry to any agent on open infrastructure: let code collect the facts, let the model reason over them, put a schema on the answer and a human in front of anything that writes. Then the model can come from anywhere.

items.title: AARO Solved Iraq's 'Jellyfish' as Balloons. Alaska's Jellyfish UFO Still Lacks the Data
items.author: Anomaly Detection
items.content:
A June sighting in Anchorage went viral in November. Two witnesses, one camera, a rainbow, a military base somewhere behind the treeline, and far more questions than verified answers.

A Rainbow, a Treeline and an Object With Tentacles

At about 10:13 p.m. Alaska Daylight Time on June 15, 2026, Sara Jane Osborn was photographing a rainbow from a car on Sixth Avenue in Anchorage when she noticed a dark, black-and-silver shape above the trees. Her husband, Pete, pulled into an empty downtown parking lot so she could shoot unobstructed. Osborn described dangling appendages that seemed to move independently as the shape turned side to side, and said it was visible for roughly three minutes before it "disappeared almost as quickly as it came," according to IBTimes UK, which drew on a November 10 Daily Mail interview.

The couple then searched a nearby park for a kite flyer and drove toward Arctic Valley, looking for about 30 minutes without finding an operator or another witness. That fruitless search is part of their testimony. It is not proof that a kite was impossible. Asked who knows what she saw, Osborn offered: "Only God and the government." She also allowed, "maybe it's a drone-type thing."

Two eyewitnesses are named: Sara Jane and Pete Osborn. Only Sara Jane is credited as the camera operator. Coverage that says the couple "captured" the object does not establish two independently operated cameras.

The defensible public count as of November 12: one witness, one phone, several still photos taken in quick succession, followed by one video, per IBTimes UK. No outlet we reviewed published the video's length or the total number of stills. The clips circulating on X and Instagram, including an X post by Mario Nawfal and a screengrab WION credits to X user @digijordan, appear to be reposts, crops or excerpts of the same encounter. Counting reposts as independent sightings would be misleading.

No verified second-angle recording was located. Nor was an original uncompressed file, complete EXIF metadata, camera specifications, verified geolocation or an authenticated radar track. WION says plainly that it "cannot independently verify the authenticity" of the footage.

five months between capture and publication is a long time for a file to travel through messaging apps and social platforms, each of which strips metadata and recompresses video. Provenance standards like C2PA can, in principle, ride along with a file, but provenance metadata is only useful if it survives, and as Paul Krause argues on HackerNoon, records attached to a file can simply be stripped. The single most valuable artifact in this story is still the original file on Osborn's phone.

Was It Over Military Land? The Map Matters

The couple believed the object sat toward Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson (JBER). Pete estimated it was within about three miles. IBTimes UK notes that neither the distance nor any link to the base or military airspace has been verified. An object visually aligned with military land may be much closer to the camera. Without a reliable range, azimuth and camera position, no one can say whether it entered restricted airspace.

The published still adds a useful constraint. In the frame, the object hangs in front of a sunlit, forested mountainside, not against open sky (see the feature image). Whatever it was, it was nearer to the camera than that slope. That fits a modest-range object at least as well as a giant distant one.

The Sun Was Up, and Behind Them

"10:13 p.m." sounds like night. In Anchorage in mid-June, it isn't. Sunset that week falls around 11:39 p.m. at an azimuth of about 328 degrees, and civil twilight runs all night. Using the standard NOAA solar-position approximation, we estimate the sun sat roughly 6 degrees above the horizon in the northwest at the time of the sighting.

Two things follow. First, a rainbow always forms opposite the sun, so Osborn was facing generally east to southeast, toward the Chugach front range, which is consistent with a sightline toward the eastern reaches of JBER and Arctic Valley. Second, a low sun behind the camera front-lights everything in view. That helps explain a "silver" sheen on a dark object. Reflective fabric, foil or Mylar would flash brightly in exactly that light.

It also rules out one famous lookalike. A "space jellyfish" is a rocket exhaust plume lit by the sun high above a ground observer who is in twilight darkness. Osborn was standing in daylight, and the object was in front of a mountainside, not 100 miles up.

Does It Really Look Like a Jellyfish?

Visually, yes, at a descriptive level. A domed upper mass with thin dangling projections evokes a jellyfish drifting through water, and the resemblance strengthens when the appendages flex and the body rotates. But resemblance is not taxonomy. Helium decorations, show kites, balloon bundles, fabric, debris and compression artifacts can all produce organic silhouettes.

Real jellyfish move by contracting a bell to push water. The Anchorage object has not been shown to pulse in a matching locomotion cycle, and the available clips do not establish its speed, altitude or any controlled acceleration. "It looked alive" is a witness impression, not a biological or aerospace finding.

The Best Ordinary Explanations, and What Each Would Need to Prove

Long fabric streamers and wind-driven rotation fit the silhouette. Inflatable octopus and jellyfish show kites are commercial products, sold in sizes like an 8-meter octopus. A visible tether, an identified operator or a weather-consistent trajectory would strengthen the case. Note that under the FAA's Part 101 rules, kites flown high or near an airport require notice to air traffic control, and Anchorage has several airports, including JBER and Merrill Field. The couple's failure to find a flyer does not eliminate the explanation, and Osborn's own reasoning ("why would you only fly it for, like, three minutes?") is a fair question rather than evidence.

Balloon cluster or novelty balloon. A buoyant object can drift and rotate while ribbons swing on their own. Close-ups showing seams or strings, or a reconstruction against wind data, would test it. This is the explanation that resolved the most famous previous "jellyfish" (see below).

Mechanically possible, but there is no evidence of a drone, operator, motor noise or flight record. Since March 2024, the FAA has fully enforced its Remote ID rule, which requires most drones to broadcast identification and location. A compliant drone would have been detectable by any nearby receiver at the time; no one has reported such a capture.

Digital manipulation or AI generation. Possible in principle, but no forensic analysis of the original file has been published either way. As HackerNoon contributor Matthew of Technology News Australia observes, despite ubiquitous cameras no one has produced one clear, independently verified photograph of an alien craft. Blurry phone footage keeps both the believers' and skeptics' cases unfalsifiable.

Perspective and apparent size. The couple recalled an aircraft that looked much smaller than the object. That comparison cannot establish size unless both distances are known. The Pentagon's AARO paper on forced perspective and parallax explains why apparently huge or fast objects routinely mislead observers.

As of November 12, no aerospace engineer, meteorologist, imaging-forensics specialist or AARO investigator has publicly authenticated or solved this recording. Claims of expert confirmation should be treated with caution. IBTimes UK states explicitly that the object's identity, location and link to the base remain unverified.

The base rate is worth knowing. AARO's FY2025 annual report, summarized by New Space Economy, counted 319 new reports. Of the 114 incoming cases it closed, 60 were balloons and 44 were satellites. The Pentagon's 2024 historical UAP review found no verified evidence of extraterrestrial technology and noted that many unresolved cases simply lack adequate data. Neither is a determination about this video.

Al Taqaddum Air Base, Iraq, October 23, 2017. The infrared "jellyfish UAP" that Jeremy Corbell released in January 2024 was filmed from a force-protection aerostat over the base. In September 2025, AARO assessed with high confidence that it was a cluster of fully and partially inflated balloons drifting with the wind at roughly 4 to 14 mph and 850 to 2,200 feet, with no heat signature from motors. It is a separate case with a different sensor and does not corroborate Anchorage, but it is the closest precedent: dangling strings, apparent shape-shifting and a military backdrop, all resolved as balloons once the full footage and geometry were analyzed. The Metabunk forum thread documents how independent analysts reached the same answer.

Stroud area, England, February 10, 1989. Drivers near the A46 reported a jellyfish-like aerial object, according to a recap citing the Swindon Star's front page. The account rests on old newspaper reports, with no comparable imagery.

Fresno area, California, April 2023. A tentacled object drew comparisons to sci-fi creatures until zoomed footage showed strings consistent with a novelty kite, per the same recap. A useful cautionary counterexample, not a debunking of Anchorage.

What Could Actually Settle the Alaska Story

The useful next steps are concrete: obtain Osborn's original phone files and full photo burst; check capture timestamps and GPS metadata; pin down the exact Sixth Avenue and parking-lot positions; reconstruct the rainbow and mountain sightlines (the solar geometry above is a start); identify the lens focal length; pull wind profiles at several altitudes; check FAA records, Part 101 kite notices and any Remote ID logs; request a JBER public-affairs response; and look for other cameras pointed east that evening.

The open question is not whether the silhouette is strange. It is. The questions are whether the object was near or far, how it moved relative to the wind, whether its disappearance was real acceleration or just loss of visibility, and whether anyone else filmed it. Until those are answered, the most precise description is "an unidentified object in one witness's video," not an alien vehicle over a military base.

The Anchorage jellyfish is real as a reported encounter: a named woman and her husband say they saw something unusual, and her imagery surfaced five months later. The viral claims, including giant size, flight directly over JBER, impossible motion, multiple independent films and extraterrestrial origin, remain unverified. The one still in public view places the object in daylight, front-lit by a low sun, in front of a mountainside. The last famous jellyfish turned out to be balloons. This one deserves the same patient analysis, starting with the original file.

The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports: The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.
 
[...] Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system's coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News. The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

items.title: Packaging Innovation for Good
items.author: Brian Wallace
items.content:
The European Union has declared an ultimatum against unsustainability: all consumer packaging placed on the EU market must be designed for recycling by 2030.  This mandate was announced by the and formally became law in all 27 EU member states on Aug. 12, 2026.  Since then, the mandate has placed restrictions on synthetic “forever chemicals” (PFAS) in food packaging as part of the “Design for Recycling” (DfR) framework, which will become the baseline by 2030.  It is significantly reshaping how companies design, import and sell products globally.

All packaged products must meet these regulatory changes, not just those manufactured in the EU.  Because many brands prefer to standardize packaging across different nations’ markets, it is probable that PPWR’s influence will reach well beyond Europe as brands change their designs to streamline operations.

Under PPWR, materials will be graded based on their recyclability performance rates through the DfR framework.  Grade A materials are __≥95% recyclable__and meet the highest circular life cycle standards.  Grade B materials are ≥80% recyclable and are still considered to be highly efficient.  Materials graded as C are ≥70% recyclable.  Any material rated below 70% is deemed unrecyclable and will be banned from all markets.

The new rules imply that paperboard is one of the best materials for long-term reuse, reducing and recycling because it combines a high recyclability rate and excellent compatibility with set content targets.  This paper-based material can be recycled 5-10 times into innovative packaging for consumer retailers and their customers.  After it is responsibly disposed of, the cycle starts again for this valuable material.  European waste systems reportedly recover 87% of paper and paperboard packaging for reuse.  This significantly outperforms plastic, which has just a .  Other fiber-based materials help companies adjust to the tightening restrictions and mandates on single-use plastic packaging while simultaneously supporting enduring goals made for resource efficiency and overall recyclability.

The first rising concern about single-use plastics began in the 2010s.  By 2022, the European Commission proposed PPWR to replace the outdated Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive (PPWD) of 1994.  By February 2025, PPWR went into full effect.  In the coming years, the development of secondary legislation will start.  By 2028, mandatory standardized labels will appear on consumer packaging and on all waste sorting receptacles. Later on in the early 2030s, all packaging in the EU, whether locally produced or imported, will officially meet DfR criteria.  Most plastic packaging and plastic parts will meet initial minimum recycled content requirements.  By the end of the decade, all packaging must meet even stricter criteria for recyclability to ensure an even more sustainable world.

The PPWR intends to set a binding packaging waste reduction target of .  Brands that adapt to the DfR mandates from the start by adopting paperboard material and designing for a circular material lifecycle will be better prepared for decades to come.  Additionally, they will also gain an advantage in a competitive market where environmental sustainability is rapidly becoming the criterion.

items.title: AMD Zen 6 SMT Proves Very Advantageous Even For 256 Core EPYC 9996
items.author: Michael Larabel
items.content: <article>With the now-shipping AMD EPYC 9006 "Venice" SP7 server processors sporting up to 256 Zen 6(C) cores per socket, or 512 cores in a 2P configuration, you may be wondering if Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT) is still worthwhile on these increasingly high core count processors. Long story short, SMT on AMD Zen 6 is still definitely worthwhile from a performance and power perspective. I was curious myself and ran some benchmarks to explore the SMT impact on the 256-core EPYC 9996 as well as the 96-core high frequency EPYC 9686F processors.</article>
